name: Login & authentication
description: How a product gates access. Clinical software carries constraints consumer software does not: shared workstations, shift handover, badge readers, and audit requirements that make the session itself a regulated object.

name: Dashboard & home
description: The first screen after sign-in. Reveals what each vendor believes the user came to do: start an exam, clear a queue, or read yesterday's backlog.

name: Worklist
description: The queue of exams waiting to be acquired, reviewed or signed. The densest table in clinical software, and the screen where status vocabulary and triage priority get designed.

name: Patient registration
description: Entering or retrieving patient identity before an exam. Where manual typing, barcode scanning and HIS/EMR lookup compete, and where wrong-patient error is designed against.

name: Live acquisition
description: Real-time signal during recording, before anything is stored. Carries the highest time pressure of any screen in the product and the most aggressive feedback requirements.

name: Calibration & lead placement
description: Electrode contact quality, lead-off indication, gain and speed settings. The screen that decides whether the recording is usable at all.

name: ECG viewer
description: Where the trace is actually read. The signature screen of the category, and the one with the widest design variance: lead selection placement, caliper behaviour, grid rendering and scroll model all differ product to product.

name: Measurements & interpretation
description: Automatic measurements, interval tables and algorithmic interpretation statements. Where the product decides how much confidence to project about its own conclusions.

name: Holter analysis
description: Ambulatory ECG review: full disclosure, beat templates, arrhythmia episodes and 24-hour trends. Reviewing hours of signal creates navigation problems that resting ECG never faces.

name: Stress test
description: Exercise protocol screens: stage timing, treadmill or ergometer control, ST trend and blood pressure prompts. The only screen in the category driven by a live protocol clock.

name: Report editor
description: Composing the diagnosis: findings, conclusion text, templates and phrase libraries, then signature. The screen where clinician time is actually spent and saved.

name: Report output
description: The printed or exported artefact and its preview. Constrained by paper format and print layout in ways the on-screen viewer is not, and often the only part of the product a referring physician ever sees.

name: Search & filters
description: Finding a prior exam across patients, dates, devices and status. Determines whether serial comparison is a realistic workflow or a theoretical feature.

name: Settings
description: Filters, lead format, print layout, algorithm thresholds, department defaults. The screen where a product's assumptions about who configures it become visible.

name: Users & permissions
description: Accounts, roles and signing authority. In clinical software this is a regulated surface: who may sign a report is a compliance question, not a preference.

name: Connectivity & integration
description: HL7, DICOM, FHIR, PACS and EMR configuration, plus device pairing and network setup. Usually the least designed screen in the product and the one that blocks deployment most often.

name: Onboarding & wizards
description: First-run setup, guided flows and step-by-step task assistance. Shows which tasks the vendor expects the user to be unable to complete unaided.

name: Errors & alerts
description: Lead-off warnings, signal quality failures, storage and transmission errors. In a regulated device the wording of these screens is a safety artefact, not copy.
